name: Parthenon
style: Classical Greek · Doric with Ionic elements
significance: Pericles’ Acropolis building programme expressed Athens’ religious identity and political power.
lookFor: Read the ring of Doric columns, pediments and surviving sculptural details as a temple designed around Athena’s sanctuary.
constructionNote: Dates cover the Classical building and decoration. The surviving ruin includes ancient damage, later transformations and modern conservation.

name: Pont du Gard
significance: Its aqueduct supplied Nemausus, today’s Nîmes, with water from near Uzès over a route about 50 km long.
lookFor: Follow the three stacked levels of arches upward to the narrow water channel at the top.
constructionNote: The operator dates the aqueduct to around 50 CE; this is an approximate construction date, not a precisely documented year.

name: Colosseum
significance: Vespasian and Titus made public spectacle a monumental expression of imperial authority.
lookFor: Compare the stacked column orders, repetitive arches and exposed underground corridors with the oval arena above.
constructionNote: Dates mark the main construction to Titus’ inauguration; Domitian and later emperors added structures and decoration. Much of the original cladding is gone.

name: Pantheon
style: Imperial Roman · concrete dome and Corinthian portico
significance: A cylindrical rotunda carries a vast Roman concrete dome whose diameter equals the interior height.
lookFor: Stand beneath the oculus and compare the coffered dome with the classical columned porch outside.
constructionNote: The museum dates the present form to Hadrian’s reign. Agrippa’s earlier building dates to 27–25 BCE; the monument became a church in 609.

name: Hagia Sophia
civilization: Eastern Roman / Byzantine Empire · Justinian I
significance: The imperial church of Constantinople combined a huge domed interior with a basilican plan.
lookFor: Trace how the central dome connects to the supporting piers through curved triangular pendentives.
constructionNote: Dates refer to the current church’s initial construction. Repairs, buttresses, mosaics and Ottoman minarets belong to later phases; the building is now a mosque.

name: Mosque–Cathedral of Córdoba
style: Andalusian Islamic · later Gothic and Renaissance layers
civilization: Umayyad Emirate and Caliphate of Córdoba · al-Andalus
significance: Successive enlargements recorded Córdoba’s growth from an emirate capital into a caliphal centre.
lookFor: Compare the repeated red-and-white double arches and ornate mihrab with the later cathedral crossing.
constructionNote: Operator chronology: original mosque 786–788; enlargements 833–848, 962–966 and 991–994. Catholic dedication followed in 1236; the cathedral crossing began in 1523.

name: Santiago de Compostela Cathedral
style: Romanesque · later Renaissance and Baroque additions
civilization: Medieval kingdoms of León and Castile · Christian pilgrimage
significance: A major pilgrimage destination supported by bishops and monarchs, built to accommodate devotion to Saint James.
lookFor: Find the medieval stone interior and sculpted Portico of Glory behind the much later exterior façades.
constructionNote: Romanesque construction began in 1075 and the basilica was consecrated in 1211. Renaissance cloisters and Baroque façades changed its appearance without replacing the medieval core.
sourceName: Santiago Cathedral · Official history and art

name: Chartres Cathedral
style: French High Gothic · earlier and later elements
civilization: Medieval Kingdom of France · Capetian period
significance: The cathedral’s Gothic structure allowed towering vaults and an exceptional ensemble of stained glass.
lookFor: Connect the pointed arches, ribbed vaults and exterior flying buttresses to the large stained-glass windows.
constructionNote: Dates describe the main rebuilding after the 1194 fire. Earlier western elements survived; the two spires belong to different construction phases.

name: Alhambra · Nasrid Palaces
style: Nasrid Andalusian Islamic · palace and fortress
significance: A fortified court on Sabika Hill preserves the palaces and ceremonial spaces of the Nasrid rulers.
lookFor: Study carved stucco, geometric tilework, courtyard water and the intricate muqarnas vaults.
constructionNote: The selected span starts with Muhammad I’s reconstruction and ends with Muhammad V’s second reign. Buildings also predate and postdate this phase; Christian additions include Charles V’s palace.
sourceName: Patronato de la Alhambra y Generalife · History

name: Florence Cathedral & Brunelleschi’s Dome
style: Italian Gothic body · Early Renaissance dome
civilization: Florentine Republic · rise of Renaissance culture
significance: Brunelleschi’s masonry dome solved the challenge of spanning the cathedral’s enormous octagonal crossing.
lookFor: Contrast the cathedral’s Gothic arches with the dome’s eight marble ribs and twin-shell construction.
constructionNote: The cathedral began in 1296 and was consecrated in 1436; the dome was built 1420–1436. The elaborate front façade is 19th-century neo-Gothic.
sourceName: Opera di Santa Maria del Fiore · Cathedral

name: Jerónimos Monastery
style: Manueline · Late Gothic with Renaissance elements
civilization: Kingdom of Portugal · Avis dynasty and maritime expansion
significance: Manuel I’s royal monastery joined dynastic commemoration with spiritual support for departing seafarers.
lookFor: Inspect the sculpted south portal, slender church columns and densely decorated cloister arches.
constructionNote: Official accounts place the start in 1501 or 1502 and describe roughly a century of works. Renaissance and Mannerist campaigns followed Manueline work; later restorations altered the complex.

name: St Peter’s Basilica
significance: Successive papal commissions made the basilica a major project for Bramante, Michelangelo and other leading architects.
lookFor: Compare the monumental dome and classical proportions with the theatrical scale of later Baroque decoration.
constructionNote: The current basilica replaced Constantine’s fourth-century church. Its construction ended in 1626; Bernini’s square and other decorations followed.
sourceName: St Peter’s Basilica · Official construction history

name: Palace of Versailles
civilization: Kingdom of France · Bourbon monarchy, Louis XIV
significance: The palace became the main royal residence and centre of government in 1682, concentrating court life around the king.
lookFor: Read the long symmetrical façades, Hall of Mirrors and garden axes as a coordinated display of royal power.
constructionNote: The selected span covers Louis XIV’s transformation of an earlier hunting château. Louis XV, Louis XVI and later museum conversions added further layers.

name: Sagrada Família
civilization: Modern Catalonia · civic patronage and Catholic devotion
significance: Gaudí transformed an initial neo-Gothic church project into a distinctive, long-running experiment in structure and symbolism.
lookFor: Compare the sculptural façades with the branching interior columns and the geometry of the vaults.
constructionNote: The cornerstone was laid in 1882; Gaudí took over in 1883. Interior works reached completion in 2010, but later generations continue the whole basilica. 2026 marks the current reference year, not completion.
sourceName: Sagrada Família Foundation · History of the temple

name: Eiffel Tower
civilization: French Third Republic · industrial age and world exhibitions
significance: Built for the 1889 Paris World’s Fair, the tower displayed industrial engineering at an unprecedented urban scale.
lookFor: Follow the exposed iron lattice and riveted connections from the four spreading legs to the narrowing summit.
constructionNote: Construction began in January 1887 and the structure was completed on 31 March 1889. Later broadcasting equipment and visitor facilities are separate additions.
sourceName: Eiffel Tower · Official history and construction

name: Villa Savoye
significance: Le Corbusier and Pierre Jeanneret turned a family weekend house into a demonstration of their five points of architecture.
lookFor: Find the pilotis, ribbon windows, free façades and roof garden, then follow the ramp through the house.
constructionNote: The commission and design began in 1928; the house was delivered in summer 1931. The monument has undergone later conservation and restoration.
sourceName: Fondation Le Corbusier · Villa Savoye and Gardener’s Lodge
